model:glm|title:glm models cut ai coding.content_excerpt: Revolut serves 80 million customers across 45 markets, and a secondary share sale that closed in July 2026 valued it at $115 billion, making it Europe's most valuable private company. It also, according to the man who runs its AI operations, now spends about one-tenth on AI coding tokens what it used to pay Anthropic and OpenAI. The blended cost of running self-hosted GLM models is 30 cents per million tokens, David Abitbol said on the AI Engineer podcast — and that single number is quietly rewriting how a regulated bank buys artificial intelligence. The striking part is not the discount. It is that Revolut reached it by doing less: fewer GPUs than the workload would seem to demand, less context than the models advertise, less precision than the hardware allows, and fewer permissions than an autonomous agent would want. Constraint, not capacity, turned out to be the lever. Revolut's numbers come from a sample of 2,000 engineers tracked over roughly a year, which makes them unusual — most enterprises deploying AI assistants have no clean before-and-after. The first rollout, Gemini in January 2025, delivered a 10% improvement in lead time and 20% in coding time. Abitbol credits the coding gain to engineers no longer digging through Stack Overflow and documentation. Claude Code was trialed around February 2025 and launched at scale in January 2026, but showed little measurable impact at first — and the cost raised eyebrows. Engineers were spending $1,000 to $10,000 a month with weak returns, so the rollout arrived with strict budget caps. Self-hosting open-source models from around April 2026 changed the picture. GLM 5.1 at that point delivered a 60% improvement in coding time and 70% in lead time. The asymmetry is the insight. The larger gain landed on lead time, not coding time, because writing code was never the bottleneck. "What we find is the bottleneck for engineering is not necessarily coding," Abitbol said. "You can save a lot of time not having to dig through your inbox or messing with Jira and Confluence." There is a second-order effect that does not show up in the table. When tokens are effectively unlimited, engineers stop rationing them — saving the expensive tool for the end of the quarter or the hardest task — and start using it on everything. Abitbol's posture now is blunt: open source is the priority, billing is flat with no month-to-month bill shock, and frontier models are the exception. story|title:a benchmark that diffs the w.content_excerpt: Benchmark for computer-use agents on self-hosted business apps, graded by whole-database diffs: success, collateral damage, irreversible changes, false completion. A benchmark that checks what a computer-use agent actually did to the database, not what it said it did. Agents drive real, self-hosted business apps (Invoice Ninja, Dolibarr, Odoo 17, Odoo 18) in a browser. Every episode starts from the same database snapshot, and afterwards the whole database is diffed . That gives four verdicts per episode instead of one: Agents: GPT-6 Luna (accessibility tree + screenshot) and UI-TARS-1.5-7B (screenshot only), same harness, 30-step budget. Full write-up with every table, the failure taxonomy and the limitations: reports/phase0_writeup.md . These are small-sample results from one person's Phase 0: 36 to 72 episodes per cell, one run per task, Wilson 95% intervals. Read Limitations before quoting a number. You need Docker, Python 3.10 to 3.12 (or uv , which fetches one for you), and about 8 GB of free disk. Check the published numbers without running anything (rebuilds every table from the committed episode summaries: 635 scored, plus 35 superseded ones kept for a sensitivity check): swm up takes about six minutes the first time (image download and seeding). In Phase 0, GPT-6 Luna cost one to three cents per successful task. Each episode writes screenshots, the step log and a summary.json under runs/<tag>/<task>/ . Apps: invoiceninja · dolibarr · odoo17 · odoo18 . Everything binds to 127.0.0.1 , agents cannot navigate off localhost, and no real email can be sent. A custom agent is one class with one method. It returns a BrowserGym action string: The diff lives in swm/dbdiff.py (about 90 lines, MySQL and Postgres). What counts as a legitimate change for each task is in swm/tasks_*.py . Clean condition. Full table with perturbations and per-skill breakdown: reports/phase0_results.md . Neither agent was trained on any of these apps, so this table measures app difficulty, not transfer. State-based grading of agents is an active area. Agent-Diff diffs full environment state for API agents on Slack, Linear, Box and Calendar replicas. EntWorld verifies enterprise GUI agents by querying Odoo and EspoCRM databases. WebArena and WorkArena are the standard web-agent benchmarks, and this harness is built on BrowserGym . story|title:a browser api for choosing a.content_excerpt: navigator.models is a proposed browser API for web apps that need a particular open-weight model on-device. A workflow built around one model may not work with another. Apps should be able to ask for the model they built and tested against, regardless of which browser someone uses. Web Models makes that request explicit. The page names a model ID. The browser runs that model or tells the page it can’t. There is no quiet fallback. The best model for scanning a receipt, transcribing audio, and searching documents may differ. A model ID lets a developer ask for the same model and release in any browser. Some models take gigabytes to download and plenty of memory to run. The browser can share their weights across sites, so every site does not need to download and store another copy. An app asks for a model, and the browser asks the user. They can see and revoke access for each site and model. The browser also keeps an eye on setup, execution, and resource limits. When someone searches their notes or documents, they should not have to send them to a model provider. Local inference can keep that data on-device and work offline when the model and content are already there. Your app picks the model and calls the API. The user grants access. The browser runs it. This is just illustrative JavaScript. <model-id> is a placeholder. Your app provides button , output , and showFallback() . The first access request has to start with a user gesture. This page does not run a model. For a one-off task, make a direct call. If you will use the model again, keep it in a session. Your app still owns the conversation history. Once access is granted, the browser tells you what that model supports. Vision, audio, tools, structured output, reasoning, and embeddings all depend on the model you chose. Each ID is tied to fixed weights, a tokenizer, and default input and generation settings. A changed release gets a new ID, so developers decide when to move to it. story|title:dawn of the super agent.content_excerpt: A few months ago if you'd asked me if an agent could run Agno, I would have said NO. Impossible. Too many moving parts. The system was too complex, I hated the writing style, and we had to be involved in the design decisions. But around september, we noticed a step change improvement in how coding agents made decisions. They went off on fewer tangents, made better design decisions and were more thorough in their work. Astra's even half-decent at writing docs. I started trusting them with more ambitious work. Now I use one super-session to coordinate everything. I still run my agents manually, pass context between them, check for reviews and take things to the finish line. But that one long-running super-session is my partner in crime. Now the question is: can I hand over this coordination to a super-agent? Can a super-agent eventually run Agno for me? I'm at the beginning of this journey so if your team is spending more and more time managing agents, follow along. A Super Agent sits on top of your coding agents and coordinates their work. You give it an outcome, it figures out what to do, which agents to use and how to get it done. Today I do all of this manually. It makes sense to take this step by step, so here's what I'd consider a success for Super Agent v1: This is a big time sink that super can take over. I do most of my development using coding agents. Claude or codex will write the spec, I'll review the design, they'll implement it and run tests. Once the PR is up, I ask claude and codex for reviews, take their findings back to the original agent and ask it to fix what's valid and relevant. No nitpicking. Then we review again and repeat a few times. I want to hand over the whole coding-agent orchestration to super and get back a PR that's ready for merge. As of today Agno has 950 open issues. Whenever a new issue opens, I want super to kick off codex, reproduce it, figure out what's going on. If it's a bug, write a failing test, work on a fix. If it's a question or an issue that's been fixed, answer it and close the issue. If it's a new feature worth considering, propose a Project (see #5). Agno has a lot of moving parts and we test the framework using cookbooks and tests. Super can keep the cookbooks up to date as the framework changes. Today I coordinate a lot of this manually. story|title:gavel guided code review wit.content_excerpt: Review local Git changes in your browser with Claude Code or Codex . The gavel skill tells your agent to prepare a brief, explain its choices beside the code, and guide you through the diff. Large changes are split into focused reviews, so you have less context to hold in your head at once. Ask questions in threads, request revisions, and give each part a verdict. As a background task, I’ve been working for … longer than I’d like to admit on the task of adding authentication and authorization to PhotoStructure. The fourth (!!) dev spike was the charm—the first three attempts left me with a pretty solid set of specifications to guide the implementation. I wrote the db schema and the onboarding flow. Claude and Codex helped flesh out the implementation over several hundred sessions, coordinated with technical project plans . I reviewed every change before committing it. And it’s been a slog . It’s a given that authentication and authorization are going to be hard. But I felt like my reviewing approach kinda sucked had a lot of opportunity for improvement. It’s a bit of a PITA. My brain only has so many thinks it can think in a day. Any friction to giving the robot feedback, especially as your brain fades, can let “fuck it, ship it” creep in. I was explaining this to my wife during a walk, and realized that there was a better way. At a prior job at a Big Company, I helped interns get their PRs approved and merged by having them write a narrative around their diffs . This approach helps walk the reviewer through the PR, and is way better than the asciibetical sort order of staged diffs and a proposed git commit message that I’d been slogging through. The reviewer spends their limited cognitive mojo on judging the PR, not on basic orientation and background arcana. If the agent could write a “brief” for every review–just a sentence or three–and then add linked comments through the diffs to walk me through the changes, each review would be much simpler to digest and wrap my brain around. But, ugh, agents still work via a glorified chat interface. The Codex and Claude desktop apps, for example, each have a diff tool, but neither threads your comments. Juggling multiple issues simultaneously in one review is work . I’ve also seen the Codex diff viewer get confused and show irrelevant diffs from other worktrees. The Codex iOS app is supposed to show diffs, but that hasn’t worked for me, and the Claude iOS app doesn’t even have diffs afaict. I looked for an open sou

story|title:trustgraph acls that follow.content_excerpt: Policy-as-code for what AI agents produce: decide where an agent's output can go, based on what it read. Policy-as-code for what AI agents produce. Decide where your agent's output can go, based on what it read. Permission systems decide what an agent may read . They lose track the moment the agent writes something new. In May 2025, Invariant Labs showed a coding agent reading a user's private repositories and publishing what it found in a pull request on a public one, after it read a crafted issue. Every step was something the agent was allowed to do. Reading private code was fine. Opening a public pull request was fine. Nothing checked that the second came from the first. Taking away access does not fix this: the agent needs the private code to do its job. What is missing is a rule about where things derived from it may go. The same gap opens each time one agent hands its work to another: the restriction should follow the data through every step. You write one small policy file. It says who may read anything derived from each source, which agents may use it, and where each action sends output: TrustGraph records what each output was built from, through every step, and answers allow , needs approval or deny with the reason: Approval adds a requirement. It never widens who may read a source. Anything the policy does not name is denied. A policy carries its own tests. Each one states what the agent read, what it tries to do and the answer you expect. Read a policy back in plain English, see exactly who gains access when it changes, and run it through the simulator: Every command takes --json . There are six worked policies in examples/policies . TrustGraph assumes an agent drafts the policy and a person approves it. Every problem is reported at once with a path, a stable code and a suggestion, so an agent can run the loop init → check → test → simulate → explain → diff on its own. A person then reviews the plain-English explanation and a diff in which every widening of access is marked. Point your agent at docs/agents/writing-policies.md or llms.txt . Protect the policy file with code review. Status. The policy CLI, trustgraph serve and trustgraph gateway have been through security review; the gateway's assumptions are listed in docs/gateway.md .
